outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] Explain a function from the workspace
outcomes.prose:
`debounce` delays calling `fn` until `wait` milliseconds have passed without another call. Each new call cancels the previous timer, and only the latest arguments are used.

Use it when you want one action after a burst finishes—for example, sending a search request after the user stops typing or handling window resizing after resizing ends.

Use throttling when you need calls to happen periodically during a continuous burst, such as limiting scroll or mouse-move handlers to once every 100 ms.

outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] Explain a function from the workspace
outcomes.prose:
`debounce(fn, wait)` in `src/timing.js` returns a wrapped version of `fn`. Each call to the wrapper cancels any pending timer and starts a new `wait` ms timer. `fn` only runs once calls have stopped for `wait` ms, and it runs with the arguments from the last call.

Some limits of this implementation:
- It is trailing-edge only. There is no immediate "leading" call.
- It has no `cancel` or `flush` method.
- It doesn't preserve `this`, because the wrapper is an arrow function.
- It discards the return value of `fn`.

**Debounce vs. throttle**
- **Debounce** waits for a burst of events to end and then fires once. Use it when only the final value matters:
  - search-as-you-type requests
  - autosave after typing stops
  - validating a form field
  - recalculating layout after a window resize ends
- **Throttle** fires at most once per interval while events keep coming. Use it when you need regular updates during continuous activity:
  - scroll or drag handlers
  - mousemove tracking
  - progress or analytics pings

Debounce can starve. If events never pause for `wait` ms, `fn` never runs. If you need steady updates during the activity, use throttle.

outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] A one-line question gets a one-line answer
outcomes.prose:
**418 I'm a teapot.** It comes from RFC 2324, the Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol, an April Fools' joke from 1998. A teapot returns it when it's asked to brew coffee. RFC 7168 later extended the joke to teapots that handle tea requests.

The code isn't meant for real use. Some servers return it on purpose as an Easter egg. Others use it to turn away unwanted automated traffic.
